utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move on to the next witness, I would like to clarify a particular matter. Yesterday you asked me, in connection with Witness K21, when this proposal was presented in terms of 92 bis -- my answer to you was that I expected to get the statement of that witness yesterday afternoon, and indeed I did get it yesterday afternoon. I read the statement, and I would like you to take into consideration some facts which indicate that there is no reason, absolutely no reason whatsoever, for that witness to be a protected witness. That witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with that. We've got a witness here. We'll look at that in due course, K21, but let's get on with the evidence now. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Dr. Shukri Gerxhaliu?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Gerxhaliu, were you born on the 23rd of August, 1953?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Studime e Poshtme in the municipality of Vushtrri in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that village now called Martiret?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Martiret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Martiret. Thank you. Dr. Gerxhaliu, from the 17th to the 19th of February, 2000, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 4th of February of this year, 2002, in the village of Martiret, in the municipality of Vushtrri, Kosovo, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you made in February 2000, in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you confirm at that time that the copy of the statement that was provided to you was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would offer that statement into evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dr. Shukri Gerxhaliu has lived most of his life in the village of Studime e Poshtme, or Martiret, in the municipality of Vushtrri in Kosovo. He is married, with four children. He has worked as a medical doctor in the hospital in Vushtrri and currently holds the post of occupational health specialist. Beginning around October 1998, Dr. Gerxhaliu also treated the KLA wounded, either at his home or in villages held by the KLA, and he also treated members of the civilian population in those villages who needed medical assistance. Dr. Gerxhaliu describes how, after the NATO bombing campaign began, Serb forces launched an offensive from the village of Rashice, beginning on the 28th and 29th of March, 1999. The offensive included shelling of the village where Dr. Gerxhaliu lived with his family. Dr. Gerxhaliu's family and other residents of Studime e Poshtme --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Dr. Gerxhaliu's family and other residents of Studime e Poshtme left their village. Dr. Gerxhaliu went into the mountains to work in the KLA field hospitals at this time. Around the 7th to the 10th of April, 1999, Dr. Gerxhaliu's family returned to their village but Serb forces arrived, searching for Dr. Gerxhaliu. At that time, Dr. Gerxhaliu decided to take his family to the KLA-controlled areas in the mountains. The witness describes how he and his family then came under fire from Serb forces as they walked to the village of Studime e Eperme and Poshtme. For the next few weeks, Dr. Gerxhaliu continued to work in the KLA field hospitals. Dr. Gerxhaliu describes how, on the 2nd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let me interrupt you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no interpretation, and it seems that Mr. Slobodan Milosevic is not getting an interpretation either. There's no interpretation into the Serbian language, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, will you sit down, please. We'll wait and see what's happened. I understand a couple of minutes should put it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Around the 7th to the 10th of April, 1999, Dr. Gerxhaliu's family returned to their village but Serb forces arrived, looking for Dr. Gerxhaliu. At that time, Dr. Gerxhaliu decided to take his family to the KLA-controlled areas in the mountains. The witness describes how he and his family came under fire from Serb forces as they walked to the village of Studime e Eperme. For the next two to three weeks, Dr. Gerxhaliu continued to work in the KLA field hospitals. Dr. Gerxhaliu describes how, on the 2nd of May, 1999, following a breakthrough of Serb forces at the front lines in the villages near Llap and Meljanica, the civilians who had sought refuge in the mountains decided to form a convoy and head down the mountain in the direction of the town of Vushtrri. Dr. Gerxhaliu estimated that there were around 40.000 people in the convoy. The convoy set off in the afternoon of the 2nd of May, and Dr. Gerxhaliu describes how the convoy moved very slowly and came under fire from Serb shelling. He saw many wounded people. The witness hid under plastic sheeting in the trailer he was riding in to avoid recognition on the approach of Serb forces to the convoy. He describes Serb soldiers and paramilitaries repeatedly approaching the people on the convoy, demanding money from people and shooting men who had none. Dr. Gerxhaliu's wife was threatened with rape until she handed over several hundred Deutschmarks to one of the Serbs. From where he lay in the trailer, Dr. Gerxhaliu heard as Serbs questioned and beat his brother-in-law Halil and saw and heard when Serb forces shot and killed the man who drove a tractor behind that of the Gerxhaliu family. Dr. Gerxhaliu heard two men speaking in Serbian next to his trailer. One said, "How many have you killed already?" Another voice said, "About 50." The first voice said, "Let's continue until we reach a hundred." The Serb forces killed the men in the convoy who did not satisfy their demands for money. Fearing for their lives, Dr. Gerxhaliu and his brother-in-law Halil ran away from the convoy and hid in a nearby stream. Dr. Gerxhaliu's wife convinced the Serb forces who approached their tractor and trailer that the men in their family had already been killed. At around 11.45 on that same night, the survivors in the convoy moved on. From where Dr. Gerxhaliu and his brother-in-law Halil were hiding, they saw about ten vehicles come up the road from the south, from the direction of Studime e Poshtme. Dr. Gerxhaliu saw that two to three of the vehicles were Serb police vehicles and the remainder were armoured personnel carriers. The vehicles had their headlights on and appeared to be searching the area. Eventually, Dr. Gerxhaliu heard a voice shout in the Serb language, "Soldiers, let's go back now. We have no fuel and it is clear up here." After the Serb forces left the area, Dr. Gerxhaliu and his brother-in-law walked up towards the village of Studime e Eperme and then on to the village of Slakovce, which had been completely burned. Subsequently, Dr. Gerxhaliu and his brother-in-law walked back down the mountain to Studime e Eperme, where the massacre had occurred. At that time, some KLA soldiers were helping to bury the dead. Dr. Gerxhaliu saw some of the victims, and many of them had wounds which made them unrecognisable. Dr. Gerxhaliu was shown a list of the dead which, at that time, had 97 names on it. At the request of the KLA, Dr. Gerxhaliu returned to work at their field hospital at Slakovce. On the 29th of May, he returned to his home to see his family. On the 31st of May, 1999, Serb police were seen in the nearby courtyard of Dr. Gerxhaliu's cousin, Seladin Gerxhaliu. Dr. Gerxhaliu fled to avoid arrest. As he fled, Dr. Gerxhaliu heard voices swearing and shouting in the Serbian language and he heard gunshots. Other neighbours reported seeing seven Serb policemen in the area, as well as three bodies. Dr. Gerxhaliu later saw that these three bodies were those of his relatives - and I apologise if I mispronounce these names - Xhemel Gerxhaliu, Seladin Gerxhaliu, and Seladin's son Shaban. Dr. Gerxhaliu saw bullet wounds on these three bodies. Another relative, Fatbardha Gerxhaliu, brought a camera and photographed the bodies, and the Serb authorities were called. After a judge, a doctor, and some Serb policemen attended the scene and then left, Dr. Gerxhaliu entered the house of his cousin Seladin. There he discovered the dead bodies of nine members of his extended family, including several children under the age of 12. All of them had apparently been shot to death. One or two days later, on about the 4th or 5th of June, the remainder of the Gerxhaliu family, including this witness, left for Montenegro, where they stayed for two weeks, until NATO troops entered Kosovo later in June 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. I have my statement -- I don't have my statement here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You can have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the microphone is on now. I shall start with the event that the witness described as an attack against civilians. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement - this is on page 1, the last paragraph - you said that 80 per cent of the territory of the municipality of Vucitrn was under KLA control. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That's right. I believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on, on page 2, you talk about major concentrations at Bajgora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Of whom in Bajgora?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The KLA was also at Bajgora. There was a KLA headquarters there. Or are you perhaps claiming that it wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I can talk about the municipality of Vushtrri, but Bajgora does not belong to the municipality of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's not waste any time on that. I am just dealing with your statement. On page 2, in the last paragraph, you say that you were given orders, or rather, it says quite specifically: "On the 2nd of May, the order came for the KLA to move ..." That's what it says here. I imagine it's supposed to say "withdraw." "... because the Serbs had broken through the front line." How long did this fighting go on?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I'm not a military officer, and I wasn't on the front line at that time; I was at the hospital. But I know that there was fighting there and that on the 2nd of May, because of the breakthrough at the front and because of the lack of food and other things, on the 2nd of May, faced with shells that went over our head, we headed off in the direction of Ceceli and then in the direction of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to your statement, 80 per cent of the territory was under KLA control. Fighting took place where there was a front line, according to your statement. According to your statement, our forces broke through the front line and then you withdrew - the KLA, that is - and you who were the non-combatants but certainly the KLA as well. You worked as a physician for the KLA, didn't you? And you were withdrawing in some direction. It's not important at this moment in which direction it was. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said all that in his statement, or just in the evidence, so let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the operations that he describes are operations against the KLA. Among them was the doctor who treated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are not operations against the civilian population. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're putting - so that we can understand it - that the operations of the Serb forces were against the KLA and not against the civilian population. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I put it very clearly what this was all about. He described the situation by saying that 80 per cent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't go over it again. Let the witness answer. What is suggested - and you can answer from your experience - is that this operation was an operation against the KLA and was not aimed at civilians. Now, can you help us if that's right or not? If you can't help us, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operation, after the front fell, they started in the afternoon against civilians, because they didn't aim at the soldiers over there on the eastern part, but precisely on the convoy of civilians. I'm talking about what the Serbian forces did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Our forces were searching the convoy after this fighting and after the front fell. That's what you said; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Serbian forces from behind, from Melenice and the north, followed the convoy, whereas there were other forces up ahead. So that the convoy was surrounded on all sides, until 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, and then the night of terror began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A group of the KLA were withdrawing with the convoy; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you were the only KLA member in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. I was by myself there. I was unarmed and without uniform. I only had my scalpel and medical equipment. That was the only armament that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Were you the only member of the KLA in that convoy of 40.000 persons who were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that the KLA was not withdrawing with civilians and that it did not take civilians as their human shield, which was their usual practice?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This is absolutely untrue. The KLA was towards the east, by Dumnice, whereas the civilians were undefended nearly, and I was there with my equipment, with my stethoscope and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's also suggested that the KLA took civilians as their human shields. Did the KLA do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it didn't do that. I never saw anything of that kind. That is quite untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is also suggested that it was their usual practice. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true. The soldiers took the wounded to safe places, whereas civilians, because of lack of food and other things, and the shelling, were forced to go to Vushtrria, head in that direction in the hope of going abroad somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, please don't interrupt my cross-examination, because it has a certain logic of its own, and I want the witness to answer one question after the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He will answer one question after the other, and the logic will appear if you refrain from asking more questions than one. What you do is you bind up in what you call a single question three or four points, such as this one about the KLA taking human shields, as is their usual practice. Ask one question literally and we'll get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we're going to move on faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just now this was a convoy of unprotected civilians because the KLA had gone to the other side. My question is quite simple. It contains only one question: Why did the KLA leave the civilians unprotected?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The KLA had gone to another strategic point and protected the wounded and the sick, but there were so many civilians without food or medicines, and so they were just compelled to let them go if they were to survive, and to give them a chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that they had some other wounded and sick civilians along with the civilians whom you had in the convoy, that there were some other civilians there with them too?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Where do you mean that there were other civilians?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. I don't believe that there were civilians with the KLA. They told me, "If you want to stay with the wounded, we will stay and stand by them to the end and not hand them over alive. But I went with my family and returned to them and headed in the direction of Vushtrria in the hope of surviving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the convoy, did you take with you those wounded persons, the wounded KLA members and the KLA members who had been killed, or did you leave them?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. They went -- there was one person killed, and he was buried in the morning, and I was there, but the civilians were without any of the wounded, any of the -- or any ill persons until the Serbian forces arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you perhaps leave those who had been killed along the way, the members of the KLA, while your convoy moved ahead? Did you leave them by the way? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. You should read clearly in my statement that only one member of the KLA was buried that morning, and the entire convoy, until the Serbian military and police forces arrived at Studime, not one of the members of the convoy was injured or sick in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That one KLA member. Are you saying that just that one was in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, no. This man of the KLA was buried in the morning. Of the -- from the KLA, there was only myself. The others were civilians. And I was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about that one who was buried? Was he also a civilian?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: He was a soldier, and he was buried in the morning before the Serbian forces came. He had been a soldier and he was buried with honours. This is written in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did it come about that this soldier was with you when you say that there were no soldiers with you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: You're mixing things up, because the soldier was buried in the morning because of the wounds that he received on the front, while the convoy set off after 1.00 and had passed through several villages. The man was buried in Cecelia, but we had passed through Cecelia and had gone to Studime e Eperme and Serbian forces arrived later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that means that that morning you separated. You became separated from the KLA. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there when the soldier was buried, and that was where the KLA was. Then you separated later on and the civilians moved on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this now for five or ten minutes. I don't think we're getting anywhere. He has explained where and when the soldier was buried.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the situation is clear when you look at precisely what you said; that 80 per cent -- about 80 per cent of the territory, which means there was frontal fighting and then there was civilians. But let's go back to the beginning of these events. You lived in Vucitrn the whole time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: At what time do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean up until the war.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I lived in my village of Studime e Poshtme, and I worked in the health centre at Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You worked in Vucitrn. And Donja Studime is, in fact, the suburb of Vucitrn, at its periphery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: It's close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the tensions begin and the violence in your area?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The violence began some time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear that someone was killed when the first incident broke out in the Vucitrn municipality?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in these things. I haven't studied them. I have been a doctor, and I didn't go into issues of who was killed and when and where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You don't know. Now, do you remember when in mid-1998, a forester by the name of Milan Zivic was killed? And he was killed with a blunt object. You are a doctor. You must have had some connection with that, at least information coming in to you. Do you remember the event? Just say yes or no to save time.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: To tell the truth, I didn't treat him, so I don't know. It's not a name or surname that I know from my village, so I can't say anything about this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember when, at the end of 1998, somebody else was killed called Momcilo Zivic? Yes or no. In the yard of his house.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall on Bajram, before the NATO aggression, when a group of masked KLA members abducted Fehmi Mulanju in front of the eyes of his family? He was an employee of the public administration for public income in Vucitrn. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. I never heard about it. Neither the surname rings any bell. I've never heard that name. I don't think that man has ever existed in the way you are describing him. We know all the families, at least in Vushtrri, but I don't know of any family with such a last name. It's untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't hear about that. He was an employee of the republican administration for public income in Vucitrn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are wasting time by continual repetition. He Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, I don't know. I think the last name must have been wrong, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I read out the surname, and the name was Fehmi Mulanju.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That's the first time to hear of such a last name. I know many people by the name of Fehmi, but not this last name. Maybe you have misinformed you [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know a man named Fehmi who was abducted in that way by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I don't know that the KLA has ever abducted anyone, but frankly speaking --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough. That's enough. So you don't know whether anybody was kidnapped. And do you know about the KLA killing anybody before the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Whom do you mean that the KLA has killed? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said you don't know anybody, and I'm thinking of Serbs and Albanians too. Do you know of any Serb or Albanian killed by the KLA prior to the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. No. I know that the KLA has been fighting on the front. I don't know whom the KLA has killed there. It didn't need to kill anyone there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from the front line, tell me: Are you aware of terrorist KLA attacks, both on Serbs and Albanians and on Romas and on other inhabitants of Kosovo? Do you know anything about any of that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I think this is all untrue. I know someone in Mitrovica who worked up to the 3rd of June, 2000. Listen well to what I'm saying. And I know that the Serb State Security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't -- no. Both of you. Both of you. We'll not get on if you interrupt. The witness has said it's untrue, so there's no point going into any more argument about it. It's his evidence we're concerned with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked in the health centre in Vucitrn; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked a shortened period, for three hours, in the Lamoks factory as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you examined workers, do you know that of the 520 employees, 270 were Albanians in that company? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I worked there for three hours a day. There were Albanians and Serbs, and I looked upon the same -- in the same way as our father of medicine, Hippocrates, told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether the majority of the employees were Albanians, of the 520 workers that worked in Lamoks?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I think you should have asked someone else about that, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, didn't you have health files for all the workers in the company, because you were the only physician that looked after their health?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I had health files, but not each and every one of them was sick and came to -- visited. I have the files even today, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot confirm that the majority of employees in Lamoks were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Maybe they were, but that was something that was of no interest to me. For me, it was of interest to look upon them in the same way, to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you left your work when the aggression, the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, began; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: On the 26th of March I was there, not when the NATO bombing started, which was so welcome for us. But on the 26th of March, the director - he was a violent man - he came to my office and he said, "Go away." I said, "Why?" And then he said, "This is what you should do, because I have orders from above, from Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment to clarify that. Where was that, Doctor? Where was it that the director came into your office and told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in his office and he came to my clinic where I was still working. He came to the door of my clinic and told me to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This was the factory rather than the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the factory was about one or two kilometres away from the hospital, where I went three days to work, working all the time in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it was the director of the hospital who told you to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The director of the hospital - he was a stomatologist - he told me. Branko Milankovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got a paper testifying to your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: He didn't give me any papers. He just told us to leave because the paramilitaries, the police, were in the corridors, there was a lot of ammunition in the cellar, there were armed forces also in the upper floors, and so we had just to leave. We were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you haven't got a decision on dismissal, and you claim that you were dismissed by the director of the hospital. Did the KLA perhaps order you to leave your work there because they needed you on the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. At that time, the KLA didn't need me, but the KLA and everyone told us, "Don't leave your work unless you are forcibly driven away," which is what happened to me. The police were in the corridor, and the director, as I told you, ordered me to leave. And when I asked him to give me a reason, he told me that he had orders from above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste time. All right. Now, how many doctors worked in the Vucitrn hospital?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: About 20, 30. I'm not sure about the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know how many doctors worked in the same hospital that you had been working in for years?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The number changed periodically. When there were Albanians in the authority, there were about 40 doctors, but because of the violence and other factors, the number of Albanians kept going down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the doctors in the Vucitrn hospital, how many of them were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: About 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 80 per cent of the doctors in the hospital - and my information says that it was even more than 80 per cent, but 80 per cent is quite enough - that means that 80 per cent of the doctors in the hospital were Albanians, and you claim that the director of the hospital, during the state of war and the bombing and the constant terrorist attacks by the KLA, gave up 80 per cent of the cadres of his hospital and told you all to leave; is that what you're claiming? The director of the hospital, in practical terms, dismissed 80 per cent of the physicians of his hospital; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. He expelled all the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What was the name of the Serbian lady who allegedly cautioned you and warned you that you were on some sort of list to be liquidated? You say this in your statement. You say you were warned by a lady that you had -- and that you had to flee. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? What does it matter what her name was?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant because I wish to call that person to testify here, because I consider that this witness is telling complete untruths. And that is why it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it also says in the second paragraph of the witness's statement, in reference to this person, in parentheses: "(I cannot remember her name.)"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you remember the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told then and now. I am a doctor, and I have to deal with many patients, and I can't remember each and every one of them. I remember she was an old Serb lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you leave the hospital because you were afraid then or because you were dismissed by the Serb director?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I said even earlier, the Serb director came to the door and ordered us to leave. He said, "I have orders for all Albanians to leave." And I was one of them. The police were present in the corridor. I said they were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that as of October 1998, you would go to treat the wounded members of the KLA during the night; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who asked you to give them medical assistance? Who called you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Often they had come to my home or have taken me there. They were sick patients. And I have given them my assistance according to the Hippocratic oath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you graduate from the faculty of medicine?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I graduated in 1982, in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you finish your specialist training?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1996. Where did you finish your specialist training for occupational medicine?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were your other Albanian colleagues trained? So you specialised, you say, in Belgrade in 1996. What about the other ones, your fellow Albanians, colleagues? Where did they get their medical training?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Wherever they could. Who had more money went to better schools and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say here in your statement that when you started treating patients, that you didn't dare -- or, rather, that they didn't dare bring them to the hospital because the Serbs would kill them. That's what you say. Now, do you know, with respect to what you said, that the Serbs would have killed a patient coming into the hospital, whether anybody who came in for treatment into the hospital was ever killed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The police checkpoints around Vushtrri, above my house and elsewhere, they prevented anyone from passing by in those zones in the north which they controlled. So as the need was, I went and offered my assistance. It was easier for one person to get through than for sick patients to be brought through such checkpoints to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the checkpoints were barricades through which nobody could pass or just checkpoints to check out documents?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Those checkpoints which were in different places, the inhabitants of those places who were in the KLA, they were very much afraid to come and ask for medical assistance in Vushtrri for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how could any doctor in the hospital know whether a civilian who had come for treatment was a KLA member or not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I think you are mixing up things. I don't know whether you are understanding me or not. I said that those who were inhabitants of the surrounding villages, who didn't have access to that Prishtina-Mitrovica road, they were afraid because once -- that if they dare, they would be maltreated and beaten up and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, only awhile ago you said that nobody could get in through these checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Of course. Those were residents of the villages who were under KLA control were beaten and maltreated very severely at these checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's why they didn't pass through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that the Albanians who lived under KLA control were treated secretly, whereas those who lived in areas that were not under KLA control were treated in hospital. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were in the KLA zone, whether they were Albanians or Serbs, were treated the same. But the others were treated on this side. And so there was a separation between the two as far as medical treatment was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that at the checkpoints, everybody was checked regardless of whether they were Serbs or Albanians. Is that what you've said?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: People were checked, but the Albanians were mistreated and the Serbs weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during 1998 and 1999, did you treat wounded soldiers and policemen too?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Whose soldiers and policemen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia. The policemen of the Serbian police who were wounded in that area. Did you treat them? You were there doing your job at the hospital. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I did indeed check them, but there were no wounded people of this kind. There were some who were ill, but as I've said several times, according to the Hippocratic oath, I treated everybody without discrimination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that you are claiming that there weren't any killed or wounded soldiers or policemen in the area of the municipality of Vucitrn. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What he said was, if you don't misrepresent the answer, that he didn't treat anybody, only some who were ill. If you want to ask him were there any policemen or soldiers killed in the municipality of Vucitrn, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any soldier or policeman killed in the municipality of Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The Mitrovica hospital might know, but we in the Vushtrria health centre only treated the ill, whereas soldiers, members of the Serbian forces, and as far as I remember, on the 8th of January, 1999, at the hands of the forces of the Operational Zone of Shala, there were -- eight soldiers were captured with all their weapons. And they asked the military officers whether they had any health needs, whether they needed any care of any kind, and they said that they didn't have any problems. And as far as I know, they were released a few days later in good health, with the help of international mediators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had asked you whether you knew, not whether you treated any such people, but whether you knew whether any soldiers or policemen had been killed, whether you had any knowledge of that before the NATO aggression in the territory of your municipality.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I stressed that I saw these eight soldiers who were armed, who were released in good health by the KLA. And the whole world knows this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that you visited them in prison in your capacity as KLA doctor, that is to say, where KLA groups were.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to visit them because there was no need. But the military officers had asked them if there were -- was a need for medical attention and they said no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any cases of killing or wounding Albanians by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. This is quite untrue. The KLA didn't kill anybody. And the war that took place was purely a frontal war. And perhaps Albanians were wounded, but no doubt the Serbian Security Services did it, because Nexhmedin Ajeti worked in the Serbian state security until 3rd of January -- June 2000, and he -- the Serbian forces killed his son. And this is an example according to the principle that the revolution devours its own children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Serbian security forces killed him in Mitrovica, and his son is alive to -- killed his son, whereas he himself, he is alive. He lives in Prishtina. He can come and testify himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he was killed by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. He was wounded, and he -- he had worked until the 3rd of June in the Serbian Security Services, in internal affairs. I don't know. He was wounded by Serbian forces. His son was wounded and has been left an invalid, and his son was also killed according to this communist principle that I quoted, the revolution devours its children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who really attacked Ajeti or do you not know? Or did you just hear about this?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Ajeti said himself that Serbian police and military forces carried out the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think that somebody who lives in Pristina now would dare state anything else?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That's how it was, because until June, he had worked in the Serbian police service and -- in that he survived. He -- he went there, and he doesn't have any problems. Prishtina is a democratic place now, under the supervision of democratic Europe. I'm -- he's only saying the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many killings take place in Pristina as compared to the situation before the NATO aggression, according to the data provided by these services of democratic Europe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is getting well beyond the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's go on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ever since you left home, that is to say, the 28th of March, and then until your return between the 7th and 10th of April, your house was empty; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: It was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that a large number of houses in Donja Studime were burned, damaged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And everything was all right with your house when you returned to it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. My house was set on fire in two places, but fortunately, it didn't catch alight fully, but it was totally looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you wrote here that your house had not been burned. You wrote in your statement that there were traces of attempts to burn it, but you don't know why they didn't burn it. That's what you said in your statement. Therefore, your house had not been burned.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: They had tried to burn it, but they had only looted it, and then they tried to burn it, without success.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that they only attempted to burn your house, but they didn't burn it, and here you say you don't know why. How come your house remained intact, when you claim that you were the first or second person on the list for liquidation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he can't answer that. He can only say what the position was. You must ask those who were responsible for the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that there was shooting all the time around your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: That's right. From the police and military forces that were on the hill above my house and on the hill of Saracak, there was continual firing from these forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firing against who?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: On our houses in Studime, from the hill of Rashice and then down below.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then this was fighting between the KLA and the army and the police; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. No. The distance from my house to the KLA zone was about five kilometres, as the crow flies. So they were fighting -- they were firing only to scare us and to expel us and to drive us out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next day, you left the house with your family, into the hills, and you went to this village of Slakovce, is that right, under the control of the KLA, that is?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that every day there was fighting there between the KLA and the army and the police; is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were clashes in Melenice, above Bajgora, up to the front line, far away in Llap, up by Sllakofc, where they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the KLA was not fighting there where it was stationed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: The KLA had positions a long way from me. I was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say that there was fighting between the KLA and the army and the police. That is to say that you had to see this to come to that conclusion, to find out about that in some other way. How come you found out, since you were so far away?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: You could hear the gunfire, and then the ill and the wounded came and I treated them. Of course I wasn't on the front line. I was part of the logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many NATO bombings there were in your area and do you know anything about the victims of that bombing?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: In our area, NATO bombed very accurately, and it only hit Serbian Yugoslav military positions, and I don't believe that there were any victims. It was amazingly precise bombing. It was wonderful. I don't think there were any casualties, but I believe that there was damage to the Yugoslav army equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that twice while you were on the tractor they would come up to your tractor and search it. Why was it only the second time that you and your cousin Halil decided to escape? Why didn't you decide to do that the first time when they came?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: They didn't come twice, but four times, and at first we could have escaped by giving them marks. But when our marks were used up, we saw Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that everybody who didn't have marks were being killed, and so we fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim that after this breakthrough at the front line, they were not looking for members of the KLA in your convoy. You say that they were looking for Deutschmarks. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Serb forces, in combination with other forces, they came and surrounded us. First they asked us for Deutschmarks, and when we didn't have any more left, they beat us and then finally would kill us. Seeing what was happening around me, when I had no more Deutschmarks, I went to that nearby stream and then I could run away from the terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, the time is now coming up. You've had an hour. But you can ask two more questions if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you heard very strong explosions on the 31st of May, when there were bombings in the vicinity of your house; is that right? You said that the barracks were bombed or something like that.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks were bombed, the barracks of the army, and the entire house heard the blast. It wasn't far away where the bombing took place; three, four kilometres. After the war, I saw the traces of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what you've said, it seems that nobody drove you away from your house, that you left your house at your own initiative. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I left my house because of the shelling and the attacks, whereas my neighbours, they -- the forces went to their houses and told them, "Leave," because the -- the neighbours told them, "Leave, because when the forces come, they will kill you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were not fleeing from the NATO bombing, then; you were fleeing from the Serbs. Did I understand you correctly? As you were fleeing from the Serbs, you escaped, no more and no less, through Serbia; isn't that right? And you say that you had no problems there. And then to Montenegro, where you had no problems either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be the last question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you have any problems in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. On the way, we had to pay Deutschmarks again, and the High Commission for Refugees took care of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to finish within five minutes' time, until the time for our break comes. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Gerxhaliu, I'm quite certain that your work did not allow you to use anything else but a scalpel. I'm quite certain that you only did your job. However, I would like to put a few questions to you related only to the events after the 25th of March. The first thing I would like to ask you is the following: It is quite clear that you said that 80 per cent of the territory of Vucitrn, where you lived and where you did your job, was under KLA control. Does that mean that you toured all these villages where treatment was necessary, primarily these KLA field hospitals that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I travelled to all the field hospitals of the KLA. I went there thanks to the stream of the village, which is -- it is in a very low place, and I couldn't be seen by the Serb forces stationed on higher hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I wouldn't have asked you about this brook, this stream, but since you've mentioned it yourself - Your Honours, on page 6 of the English version, paragraph 3 - you say that that is the stream where it is, and that it was guarded by KLA soldiers, and that that was the road that led to the mountain but that it was guarded by the KLA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: In the upper part of Studime, the stream was protected by KLA. But from Rashice onwards, it was under the absolute control of Serb forces. KLA was only in the upper part. As the crow flies, it's about six kilometres away from where my house is. The stream is very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But later in your statement, you say that precisely around this stream people got killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: On what day are you referring?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, you didn't refer to a particular date. You said that it would often happen during those several months, that around that stream there were skirmishes and that people lost their lives there.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: There weren't skirmishes along the stream in the region of Studime e Poshtme, but on the 2nd of May, there were 109 innocent civilians killed. On the 14th of May in that very stream, in the lower part in Studime e Poshtme, where there were Serb forces stationed on both sides, six Albanian civilians were killed. On the 24th of May, eight Albanian girls were killed by the Serb police forces. On the 31st of May, my cousin, my uncle, and his whole family, 12 members altogether, were killed. Three were taken out of the house and killed. His son, Seladin's son, was killed earlier by a policeman whom we knew, on the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was around that stream, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. The police and military forces were -- came together from Rashice, and often they did -- carried out what they called a check, and killed innocent civilians for no reason at all. We have photos, documents, evidence to prove, to corroborate the terror we went through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Doctor. I'm interested in the following now: When you went to these many villages, were there any village patrols there in these villages, and were these people carrying weapons or were there only KLA members there? If there were any there, can you tell us approximately how many members of the KLA there were in these villages?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I didn't see patrol -- patrols. It was not my problem how many members were in the KLA. My only problem was to take care and to treat the sick persons. That was the underlying motive of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the members of the KLA, were there people who wore civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: I was the only one dressed in civilian clothes. I don't know about the others. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two more questions. The first one has to do with the several days of fighting before the 2nd of May when the front line fell. You said that there were a considerable number of wounded persons that you had to treat that were brought to your hospital. How many wounded persons, approximately, were brought in to the place where you had to treat them?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: We had three rooms. I believe there must have been about 35, 36 wounded. Eighty per cent of them were civilians, and 15, 20 per cent were wounded and injured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were civilians when they came to see you at the hospital? None of them had any weapons, neither those who were in uniforms nor those who were in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. Those who were soldiers were, of course, donned in uniforms. They were part of a unit. The others were women, children of two years old were injured, some young girls of 15 years old. I mean, all of them were civilians who were either injured because of the shelling, because of some stray bullets or bullets aimed at them. So as I said, 70, 80 per cent of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were brought to you from the front line during those few days. I'm talking about after the 25th of March. Those are the days when the fighting took place. I'm not asking about before the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Tapuskovic could clarify who he means by the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Tapuskovic could clarify in his question who he means by the word "they" when he says, "They were brought to you from the front line." Who does he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, could you answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean precisely what the witness has been saying, Your Honours. The front line fell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we're obviously not going to get very far with this. Is there anything else you want to ask the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the following, Your Honour, in conclusion:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether there were any victims at the front line, whether there were any KLA casualties? Because yesterday we heard from a witness that there were heavy losses on the KLA side. Were there any casualties apart from this one single person who was brought in from the place where the front line was broken through?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Certainly there must have been, because if there were no victims, the front wouldn't have fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and I think it would probably take 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Really, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could I have five to ten minutes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have five minutes now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- so that we can finish the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gerxhaliu, you mentioned that around the 26th of March, you were told by the director of your hospital to go away and that the Albanian doctors at that hospital were all sent away at that time, and you said that the director's name was Branko Milankovic [sic]. Just to be clear --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Ranko, not Branko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The name was Ranko Milankovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [In English] Milenkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milenkovic. If you know, what was the ethnicity of the director of the hospital, Mr. Milenkovic?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you, Mr. Gerxhaliu, about this notion of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have with me copies of an exhibit that has already been admitted into evidence. It is map 10 of Exhibit 4. I have a number of colour copies as well as black and white copies. I would like to ask the usher's assistance if a colour copy could be provided on the ELMO, please, and then the other copies distributed around to the Judges, to the amici, and to the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gerxhaliu, if you could please take a look at the map that's been placed to your left. It's right next to you. If you can look at the actual map, Mr. Gerxhaliu. During your cross-examination, you talked about how, around the 2nd of May, word came that Serb forces had broken through along the front line, and that was in the area of Llap and a place, I believe, that is called Meljanica. I'm wondering, Dr. Gerxhaliu, if you could take a marker - I hope there is a marker or a pen on the desk near you, or perhaps the usher could provide you one - and just roughly indicate where those -- that front line or those front lines were in relation to where you were on the 2nd of May in the morning.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: You see here Sllakofc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around Slakovce, please.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: It is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around there, please. Dr. Gerxhaliu, could you put a circle where you were, approximately.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now could you draw lines representing what you knew to be roughly the front lines that were broken through on that day, if they're visible on the map anywhere.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes. The front line must have been here somewhere, Melenice, Trepca, in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the area known as --

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: A great distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the area known as Llap?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Llap is on this side, but I can't see it very well on this map. Let me look closer. It must have been here, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you draw a line roughly where Llap would have been, or the front lines near Llap?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This village Segasht and these other villages must belong to the Llap area. Melenice, Trepca on the other side. This one front line here and one there, and these two lines were broken through. The forces came together --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu. Dr. Gerxhaliu, I just asked you, please, to draw a line where the front line at Llap was. That's all I want you to do and then we'll move on. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: This was the front line. And this, I think, must have been the other front line, but it goes beyond this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would offer that exhibit now into evidence, and that can be removed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked as Exhibit 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, my last topic: You were asked whether there were members -- it was suggested to you that there were other members of the KLA in the convoy that was attacked on the 2nd of May in the evening. I would like to show a 20-second excerpt of an exhibit. This is an exhibit that has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 13/1. I would ask the audio-visual people to please start it at 530 and let it run to 550 and stop -- and there, and then I have a few questions for this witness and then I'll be done. If we could let this run for a few seconds now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And stop, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, do you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I know this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this man?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: He was Fatmir Ejup Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Fatmir Gerxhaliu a relative of yours? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Gerxhaliu older than you or younger?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: He was some ten or 12 years younger than me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he married? Did he have any children?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Yes, he was married. His wife is from Saracak, and he has left behind two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just for the record, we're looking at the body of what looks to be a male. There appears to be some blood visible on the face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this man live?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: He lived closer to the city compared to my house, in Studime e Poshtme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a rich man, a poor man, or average?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: He was an average, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Fatmir Gerxhaliu's occupation?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: Since he couldn't find a job for the state, he engaged mainly in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to the 2nd of May, 1999, was Fatmir Gerxhaliu a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI GERXHALIU
utterances.text: No. He's never been a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Gerxhaliu, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. We will adjourn now until twenty to twelve.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour, say two words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to thank you on my behalf and that of my family, which was one of the most victimised families, because today, three years ago, on the 2nd of May, 1999, my members were killed. And I take this opportunity to thank you for enabling us to come here to testify to the truth and nothing but the truth, which I am sure it will oust -- quit [as interpreted] very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Saxon. Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, is your name Fedrije Xhafa?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Xhafa, were you born on the 16th of June, 1964?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Saracak i Ulet, in the municipality of Vushtrri, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that village now called Monza?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Xhafa, on the 26th of February, 2000, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 11th of October of 2001, did you provide an additional statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of March this year, 2002, in the village of Saracak i Ulet, or Monza, in the municipality of Vushtrri, in Kosovo, were you provided with copies of the statements that you gave in February 2000 and October 2001, in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, did you confirm that the copies of the statements that were provided to you were true and correct?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would offer copies of these statements for admission into evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 124.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Xhafa attended elementary and secondary school for mathematics in Vushtrri and was trained as a tailor. Prior to the war in 1999, she did not work outside the home. Ms. Xhafa describes how, on the 28th of March, 1999, she and her family were forced to leave their house in the village of Saracak after Serb forces began to burn houses in that village. The family fled to Dubnica village and then to Samodreza village and Vesekovce village, where they stayed for five weeks. Around the 30th of April of 1999, the family travelled from Vesekovce to Slakovce, where they spent two nights. They were informed by KLA fighters that the KLA resistance had been broken in Meljanica village, in the Mitrovica municipality, to the north-west, and that the Serb forces were advancing from the north. Ms. Xhafa's family joined a large convoy of people moving towards Vushtrri. Ms. Xhafa was riding on a trailer together with 13 members of her family. Ms. Xhafa describes how Serb forces approached her part of the convoy several times. Ms. Xhafa describes how Serb forces first beat her nephew and her brother and robbed the family's valuables. Subsequently, at about 11.30 p.m., another group of six policemen wearing masks approached Ms. Xhafa's tractor. The policemen shot and wounded Ms. Xhafa's brother and shot dead her father. Ms. Xhafa describes how her family continued on foot down the mountain and eventually were directed to the agricultural cooperative buildings in Vushtrri. The next morning, the Serb police separated the men aged between 15 and 60 from the others. The men were taken to Smrekovnica prison and all those with tractors were ordered to go to Albania. Ms. Xhafa and the surviving members of her family walked to the village of Kqiq and then moved on to the village of Doberlluka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me briefly what life was like up until the war in your area. Yes, I think the microphone is on now. Tell me, please: What was life like up until the war in your area?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It was a very difficult life before the war in my village. It got more difficult every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the village of Bare, which is the centre of the Saska [phoen] region, the Partizanka firm of Uzice constructed a factory producing leather goods, and several hundred young Albanian women were employed by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the factory there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I know there was a factory, but who worked, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that that factory, in the course of 1998, became the place where the KLA were? It was the Operative Zone for Salja.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that among those forces, the KLA forces who were located in that centre of theirs there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She doesn't know about it, so there's no point asking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking her a different question, Mr. May, and that is whether she knows that among the KLA members were members of her own family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they weren't. My brother's son was a member, but he withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you heard of the name Vesel Xhafa, father's name Ahmed, born in 1958? Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it isn't a cousin of yours from that area?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We live in the village of Saracak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in the course of 1998, the KLA prison was operational in Bare?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this. I have no information about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know at the beginning of January, precisely in that prison, soldiers of the Yugoslav army were imprisoned there that had been captured by the KLA near the Stari Trg or Old Square?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She has no information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
